title: Stationary expectations from training years matched forward skill for Japanese cherry bloom and glaciers; rivers, Swiss bloom, birds and dengue lost more from level and slope changes
abstract: Question: can the forward skill of a climate-response relation be predicted from training data alone? Approach: before analysis we froze and timestamped a plan for six panels with one common pipeline: WGMS glacier balance (59 glaciers), Canadian reference river flow (223 gauges), cherry peak bloom in Japan (56) and Switzerland (79), BBS species counts on routes (3,000) and OpenDengue national dengue cases (71). Each panel used one pooled temperature and/or precipitation window (GHCN_CAMS, CRU TS 4.09), trained on early years and scored on later years. For each series we simulated a stationary relation (same coefficients, AR(1) residuals, observed later climate) to get the expected skill E0. Results: E0 separated the panels: birds had no training signal (pooled E0 0.03, observed 0.004). The observed pooled skill against the training mean was 98% of E0 for Japanese cherry (0.646 vs 0.658), 87% for glaciers, 77% for Swiss cherry, 47% for rivers and 15% for dengue. Series-level rank calibration held in 4 of 6 panels (plan required 5). Skill fell below the stationary 5th percentile in 17-27% of series for rivers, Swiss cherry and dengue. Level shifts that the climate terms missed dominated for birds and dengue; slope changes dominated elsewhere: glacier temperature sensitivity tripled, Swiss bloom sensitivity fell by a quarter while Japanese rose, and the dengue slope halved. Class labels explained more variance than E0 (R2 0.15 vs 0.06). Limitations: six panels, simple linear windows, point climate, national dengue counts without population, Gaussian AR(1) null.
